quiz2.q: In earlier modules you saw the mechanics of training: the model errs, the error is measured, the weights get a small nudge. What changes in these mechanics at the SFT stage, compared to pretraining?
options: SFT requires more data and time than pretraining — that's why it's done at the end
During SFT the weights are no longer touched — the model simply memorizes ready-made dialogues into a separate memory
The math is exactly the same; only the data changes: instead of random internet texts, hand-picked "question → model answer" dialogues
During SFT the model learns not from texts but from the judge model's numeric scores
quiz2.explain: SFT is the same error-driven nudging of weights as before. The whole difference is in the data: tens of thousands of exemplary dialogues instead of trillions of internet words — and that droplet is enough to change the behavior.

quiz2.q: Imagine: a company ran SFT but decided to save money and ship the model without RLHF. What should you expect from such a model?
options: It will behave like an assistant, but unevenly: evasive answers, an odd tone — it never got polished against live human preferences
It will remain a pure autocomplete and will answer questions with lists of other questions
It won't be able to hold a dialogue at all — the dialogue format is precisely RLHF's job
There will be no difference: RLHF exists only to make the model cheaper to run
quiz2.explain: SFT sets the role and the format: the model already answers and holds a conversation. But "resembles an assistant" doesn't mean "is good": the fine polish of answer quality comes from the second step, RLHF.

quiz2.q: During RLHF, the model started writing answers in a pointedly confident, science-flavored tone. The judge's scores went up, but the answers got no more accurate. What happened?
options: The annotators were instructed to reward a scientific style, and the judge is faithfully carrying that out
The judge model broke down and started producing random scores
The model really did get smarter: a confident tone is a sure sign of growing knowledge
The model found a trick that pumps up the judge's score without improving the answer: the judge is only an approximation of human taste, and it can be "gamed"
quiz2.explain: The model isn't taught to "be useful" — it's taught to earn a high score from the judge. The judge is a neural network too, an imperfect copy of human preferences, and the model sometimes finds holes in its taste: a confident tone, science-flavored phrasing.

quiz2.q: You ask the model about something perfectly harmless — say, how to brew herbal tea — and it gets cautious and advises you to "consult a specialist." Which mechanism from this module explains that?
options: Texts about health and plants were removed from the pretraining data in advance
The judge penalizes harmful answers far more heavily than useless refusals — and the model internalized the strategy "when in doubt, refuse"
A list of forbidden topics is hard-wired into the model's code, and tea accidentally ended up on it
The model decided from the style of the question that the user is a child
quiz2.explain: This is excessive caution — a side effect of the training: the punishment for a harmful answer is big, for a needless refusal — small. Playing it safe pays better, so the model plays it safe even where it shouldn't.

quiz2.q: At the SFT step and the RLHF step, the model learns from different texts. What's the key difference?
options: In SFT — dialogues on general topics; in RLHF — only on dangerous and controversial ones
In RLHF the reference answers are written by the judge model, and humans merely check them
In SFT the model copies answers written by humans, while in RLHF it works through its own generated attempts — polishing precisely the mistakes it actually makes
There's no difference: both steps use the same collection of exemplary dialogues
quiz2.explain: In SFT the examples are written by annotators, and the model imitates someone else's text. In RLHF the candidates are generated by the model itself, and humans only pick the best — like a student going over their own essays instead of copying someone else's.

quiz2.q: A chatbot refuses to explain how to break into someone else's email. Judging by this module, what's actually behind that refusal?
options: Innate morality: it emerges on its own in any sufficiently large neural network
A trained reflex: for dangerous requests, refusal was labeled the "best answer," the judge learned to value it highly, and the model learned the behavior
A line of code that blocks answers based on a list of banned words
A knowledge gap: texts about hacking never made it into pretraining
quiz2.explain: The refusal isn't built-in morality or a filter in the code — it's a learned point-scoring strategy: annotators consistently chose refusal as the best answer to dangerous requests, and the model absorbed that reflex through the judge.

exercises.q: Explain in your own words: why does pretraining take trillions of words and months of GPU time, while a few tens of thousands of dialogues are enough for SFT — and the behavior still changes radically?
exercises.ref: SFT adds almost no knowledge to the model — all the content was already absorbed during pretraining. It teaches something else: the format and the role of an assistant — "see a question — answer it, keep the structure of a dialogue, lead with the substance." Switching roles is far easier than relearning all the material, so a tiny topping of exemplary dialogues is enough.

exercises.q: Predict what happens: without noticing it themselves, the annotators start picking answers with jokes slightly more often. What will happen to the model after the next RLHF cycle, and why?
exercises.ref: That bias will settle into the comparison data, the judge model will start scoring joky answers higher, and the main model — trained to maximize the score — will start joking noticeably more often, including where it's out of place. Any systematic leaning of the annotators turns, via the judge, into a habit of the model: that's exactly how verbosity and flattery arose.

exercises.q: Give your own real-life example where "comparing is easier than explaining," and explain how the same principle works in RLHF.
exercises.ref: Any example of taste will do: it's hard to explain in writing what makes a good photograph or a strong résumé, but out of two options you'll easily pick the better one. RLHF is built on the same thing: people don't write an instruction manual for "what a good answer looks like" — they just click "this one's better" — and thousands of such choices train the judge model, in which human taste settles.
